Lewd
LOOD
adjective
From Old English læwede, “lay, unlearned, common,” as opposed to the clergy. From “unlettered” it drifted to “ignorant,” then to “low, base, wicked,” and only much later to the narrow modern sense of “lustful, obscene.”

Biblical Definition

In the KJV lewd means vile, base, wicked, worthless — a broad word for men and deeds of low and evil character, not the narrow modern word for the obscene. Our age hears lewd and thinks only of lust; the Authorized Version means depravity of every kind, the baseness of a corrupt heart however it shows itself. When the unbelieving Jews at Thessalonica gather a mob, they take “certain lewd fellows of the baser sort” (Act 17:5) — not lechers but ruffians, worthless and wicked men, the rabble of the marketplace stirred up to riot. Gallio at Corinth speaks of “a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness” (Act 18:14), meaning gross criminal wrongdoing of any sort, the kind a magistrate must judge. The word does at times touch uncleanness, for the fallen heart’s baseness runs that way too: the LORD rebukes Jerusalem for her “lewd way” (Eze 16:27) and names Aholah and Aholibah “the lewd women” (Eze 23:44), where the harlotry is spiritual and bodily together. But even there the root idea is not narrowly sexual; it is vileness, the base and shameful conduct of a people who have forsaken their God. So the reader must widen the word. Lewdness in the AV is wickedness at large — the low mind, the worthless life, the heart turned base. It is the fruit of the fall, and the man who would be washed of it must be born again, for no mending of manners will make a lewd heart clean.

Webster 1828 Definition

Vile, base, wicked, worthless — a broad word for depravity, not merely the obscene.

expand to see more

LEWD, wicked; vile; base; profligate; given to evil.

From Old English læwede, “lay, unlearned,” as opposed to the clergy.

The sense ran from “unlettered” to “ignorant” to “base, wicked.”

The narrow modern sense of “lustful, obscene” is a late and partial one.

“Lewd fellows of the baser sort” (Act 17:5) were worthless ruffians, not merely lechers.

Key Scripture

Act 17:5 — "But the Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar, and assaulted the house of Jason, and sought to bring them out to the people."

Act 18:14 — "And when Paul was now about to open his mouth, Gallio said unto the Jews, If it were a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness, O ye Jews, reason would that I should bear with you:"

Eze 16:27 — "Behold, therefore I have stretched out my hand over thee, and have diminished thine ordinary food, and delivered thee unto the will of them that hate thee, the daughters of the Philistines, which are ashamed of thy lewd way."

Eze 23:44 — "Yet they went in unto her, as they go in unto a woman that playeth the harlot: so went they in unto Aholah and unto Aholibah, the lewd women."

Modern Corruption

A broad word for wickedness narrowed by the modern ear to mean only the obscene.

expand to see more

The drift here is a narrowing. Lewd once covered baseness of every kind — the ignorant, the low, the vile, the wicked — but the modern tongue has shrunk it to the single sense of the lustful and obscene. So the reader meets the “lewd fellows of the baser sort” at Thessalonica and imagines lechers, when Luke means street ruffians hired to riot, worthless men of the marketplace. Restore the broad sense and the word regains its reach: lewdness is depravity at large, whatever base and shameful shape the corrupt heart takes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that narrowing, though it touches a wound the present age keeps open. Scripture does use lewd of uncleanness — Jerusalem’s “lewd way,” the “lewd women” of Ezekiel’s parable — and here the modern narrowing is not wholly wrong, only too small. The point to recover is that such uncleanness is one branch of a deeper baseness, the corruption of a nature fallen from God. Our culture treats the lewd as a matter of taste or freedom, a private appetite to be indulged without shame; the LORD names it a vileness that provokes His hand and delivers a people to their enemies. The remedy is not refinement of manners but regeneration. A base heart cannot be coaxed clean; it must be made new, and only the Spirit of holiness can do it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means base and wicked, from an old word for ‘lay, unlearned.’

expand to see more

Lewd — from Old English læwede, “lay, unlearned, common.”

From “unlettered” it drifted to “ignorant,” then to “base, wicked.”

In the KJV it means vile, worthless, wicked — men and deeds alike.

“Lewd fellows of the baser sort” (Act 17:5) are worthless ruffians.

The narrow sense of “obscene” is a late shrinking of a broad word.

Usage

"The lewd fellows of Thessalonica were base rioters, not merely lechers."

"“Wicked lewdness” before Gallio meant gross criminal wrong of any kind."

"A lewd way in the KJV is a vile way — the whole life turned base."
